## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Clean text: fix case, remove extra spaces and replace parts of strings.
2. Detect, count and extract text that matches a pattern.
3. Turn text into dates, and pull out the year, month or weekday.
4. Calculate the time between two dates.
5. Reorder, relabel and group factor levels, so tables and charts appear in a sensible order.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(lubridate)
library(forcats)
library(ggplot2)
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
```

## Part 1: Strings with stringr

Text typed by people is messy. Here are village names as they arrived from a form:

```{webr}
villages <- c("  pader camp", "PADER CAMP ", "Pader  Camp", "awach", "Awach Trading Centre")
villages
unique(villages)
```

The first three are the same place, but R sees three different values. Every function in **stringr** starts with `str_`, takes the text first and works on whole vectors.

### Fixing case and spaces

```{webr}
str_to_lower(villages)
str_to_title(villages)
str_trim(villages)           # remove spaces at the start and end
str_squish(villages)         # also turn repeated spaces inside into one
```

Combine them to standardise the names:

```{webr}
clean <- villages |> str_squish() |> str_to_title()
clean
unique(clean)
```

Five spellings are now three places.

### Length, slicing and joining

```{webr}
str_length("Kampala")
str_sub("HH001", start = 3, end = 5)     # characters 3 to 5
str_c("HH", "001")                       # join strings
str_c("District: ", c("Gulu", "Arua"))
str_pad(c(1, 25, 300), width = 3, pad = "0")   # "001", "025", "300"
```

### Detecting and replacing patterns

`str_detect()` returns `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each value, so it works inside `filter()`:

```{webr}
str_detect(clean, "Camp")
sum(str_detect(clean, "Camp"))
```

`str_replace()` replaces the first match, and `str_replace_all()` replaces every match:

```{webr}
str_replace(clean, "Trading Centre", "TC")
str_replace_all("UGX 1,250,000", ",", "")
```

The patterns above are plain text. stringr also understands **regular expressions**, a mini-language for patterns such as "any digit" or "a word at the start". You will learn them properly on Day 13. One useful example for now: `\\d+` means "one or more digits".

```{webr}
str_extract("Plot 47, Block 3", "\\d+")
str_extract_all("Plot 47, Block 3", "\\d+")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
`str_to_upper()`, `str_trim()`, `str_sub()`, `str_c()` and `str_replace()` match Excel's `UPPER()`, `TRIM()`, `MID()`, `CONCAT()` and `SUBSTITUTE()`. The difference: one line cleans the whole column.
:::

## Part 2: Dates with lubridate

On Day 5 you saw that `read.csv()` reads dates as text. Text cannot be sorted by time or subtracted. **lubridate** turns text into real dates.

### Parsing dates

Choose the function that matches the order of the parts: `y` for year, `m` for month and `d` for day.

```{webr}
ymd("2026-03-15")
dmy("15/03/2026")
mdy("March 15, 2026")
dmy(c("01-04-2026", "1 April 2026", "01.04.26"))   # many formats, one function
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Day first or month first?
`"04/03/2026"` is 4 March in Uganda and the UK, but 3 April in the United States. Always check which order your data uses, and test a date where the day is above 12.
:::

### Pulling out parts

```{webr}
d <- ymd("2026-03-15")
year(d)
month(d)
month(d, label = TRUE)
day(d)
wday(d, label = TRUE)    # day of the week
```

### Calculating with dates

Subtracting two dates gives the number of days between them:

```{webr}
ymd("2026-04-01") - ymd("2026-03-15")
as.numeric(ymd("2026-04-01") - ymd("2026-03-15"))
ymd("2026-03-15") + days(30)
ymd("2026-03-15") + months(2)
```

`floor_date()` rounds dates down to the start of a week or month, which is useful for grouping:

```{webr}
floor_date(ymd("2026-03-18"), "week", week_start = 1)   # the Monday of that week
floor_date(ymd("2026-03-18"), "month")
```

### Dates in a data frame

```{webr}
hh_dates <- hh |>
  mutate(
    date    = ymd(interview_date),
    week    = floor_date(date, "week", week_start = 1),
    weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE)
  )

hh_dates |> count(week)
```

Now you can count interviews per week, find the first and last interview with `min()` and `max()`, or plot progress over time.

## Part 3: Factors with forcats

On Day 2 you met factors: categories with a fixed set of levels. Factors control the **order** in which categories appear in tables and charts. By default, R sorts text alphabetically, which is rarely the order you want.

```{webr}
answers <- c("Agree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly agree", "Agree")
factor(answers)   # alphabetical: Agree, Disagree, Neutral, Strongly agree
```

### Setting the order yourself: `fct_relevel()`

```{webr}
likert <- fct_relevel(answers, "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", "Strongly agree")
levels(likert)
table(likert)
```

### Ordering by frequency: `fct_infreq()`

Bar charts are easier to read when bars are sorted:

```{webr}
hh |>
  mutate(main_crop = fct_infreq(main_crop)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = main_crop)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Main crop", y = "Households")
```

### Other useful forcats functions

```{webr}
fct_recode(factor(hh$has_water), "Has water" = "yes", "No water" = "no") |> table()
fct_lump_n(factor(hh$main_crop), n = 2) |> table()   # keep the 2 most common, lump the rest as "Other"
fct_rev(factor(c("low", "middle", "high"), levels = c("low", "middle", "high"))) |> levels()
```

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: Clean text

Clean the district names so that each one has no extra spaces and is in title case (for example `"Gulu"`). Save the result as `clean_districts`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_clean
#| setup: true
library(stringr)
messy <- c(" gulu", "GULU ", "arua", "  Arua  ", "mbale")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_clean
clean_districts <- messy |>
  ______() |>
  ______()
clean_districts
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex11_clean"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
`str_squish()` removes extra spaces and `str_to_title()` fixes the case.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex11_clean"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
clean_districts <- messy |>
  str_squish() |>
  str_to_title()
clean_districts
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_clean
#| check: true
if (!exists("clean_districts")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Save the result as clean_districts.")
} else if (identical(clean_districts, c("Gulu", "Gulu", "Arua", "Arua", "Mbale"))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Five spellings are now three districts.")
} else if (any(str_detect(clean_districts, "^ | $"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Some names still have spaces. Use str_squish() or str_trim().")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Names should be in title case, like \"Gulu\". Use str_to_title().")
}
```

### Exercise 2: Detect a pattern

How many of these settlement names contain the word `"Camp"`? Use `str_detect()` inside `sum()`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_detect
#| setup: true
library(stringr)
places <- c("Pader Camp", "Awach", "Unyama Camp", "Gulu Town", "Pabbo Camp", "Lacor")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_detect
sum(str_detect(______, ______))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex11_detect"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The first argument is the text (`places`) and the second is the pattern, in quotes.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex11_detect"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
sum(str_detect(places, "Camp"))
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_detect
#| check: true
if (identical(as.integer(.result), 3L)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 3 names contain \"Camp\".")
} else if (identical(as.integer(.result), 0L)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Patterns are case-sensitive. Use \"Camp\" with a capital C.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use sum(str_detect(places, \"Camp\")).")
}
```

### Exercise 3: Parse dates

These dates are written day first, as `"15/03/2026"`. Convert them to real dates and save the result as `dates`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_parse
#| setup: true
library(lubridate)
raw_dates <- c("15/03/2026", "02/04/2026", "28/02/2026")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_parse
dates <- ______(raw_dates)
dates
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex11_parse"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The order is day, month, year, so the function is `dmy()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex11_parse"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
dates <- dmy(raw_dates)
dates
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_parse
#| check: true
if (!exists("dates") || !inherits(dates, "Date")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "dates should be a Date vector. Use a lubridate function such as dmy().")
} else if (anyNA(dates)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Some dates became NA. Check the order: day, month, year.")
} else if (identical(dates, as.Date(c("2026-03-15", "2026-04-02", "2026-02-28")))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The dates are in the wrong order. These are day first: use dmy().")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Calculate with dates

Add two columns to the survey: `date`, the interview date as a real date, and `days_to_deadline`, the number of days from the interview to the reporting deadline on **2026-04-10** (as a number). Save the result as `hh2`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_days
#| setup: true
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
hh <- read.csv("data/household-survey.csv")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_days
hh2 <- hh |>
  mutate(
    date             = ______(interview_date),
    days_to_deadline = as.numeric(______ - date)
  )
hh2 |> select(household_id, date, days_to_deadline) |> head()
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex11_days"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
`interview_date` is written year-month-day, so use `ymd()`. The deadline is `ymd("2026-04-10")`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex11_days"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
hh2 <- hh |>
  mutate(
    date             = ymd(interview_date),
    days_to_deadline = as.numeric(ymd("2026-04-10") - date)
  )
hh2 |> select(household_id, date, days_to_deadline) |> head()
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_days
#| check: true
expected <- as.numeric(as.Date("2026-04-10") - as.Date(hh$interview_date))
if (!exists("hh2") || !all(c("date", "days_to_deadline") %in% names(hh2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "hh2 needs the columns date and days_to_deadline.")
} else if (!inherits(hh2$date, "Date")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "date should be a real date. Use ymd(interview_date).")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(hh2$days_to_deadline, expected))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(hh2$days_to_deadline, -expected))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The numbers are negative. Subtract the interview date from the deadline: deadline - date.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "days_to_deadline should be as.numeric(ymd(\"2026-04-10\") - date).")
}
```

### Exercise 5: Order factor levels

Survey answers should appear in a logical order, not alphabetically. Turn `answers` into a factor with the levels in this order: `"Low"`, `"Medium"`, `"High"`. Save it as `priority`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_factor
#| setup: true
library(forcats)
answers <- c("High", "Low", "Medium", "High", "Low", "High")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_factor
priority <- fct_relevel(answers, ______)
levels(priority)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex11_factor"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
List the levels in the order you want, each in quotes and separated by commas: `"Low", "Medium", "High"`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex11_factor"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
priority <- fct_relevel(answers, "Low", "Medium", "High")
levels(priority)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex11_factor
#| check: true
if (!exists("priority") || !is.factor(priority)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "priority should be a factor. Use fct_relevel().")
} else if (identical(levels(priority), c("Low", "Medium", "High"))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Tables and charts will now show Low, Medium, High in that order.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The levels should be in the order Low, Medium, High.")
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Cleaning only some of the variations.** After cleaning, run `unique()` or `count()` to check that the categories are what you expect.
- **Forgetting that patterns are case-sensitive.** `str_detect(x, "camp")` does not match `"Camp"`. Clean the case first, or use `regex("camp", ignore_case = TRUE)`.
- **Parsing with the wrong date order.** `ymd()` on day-first dates gives `NA` or, worse, the wrong date. Check a date with a day above 12.
- **Subtracting dates stored as text.** Convert with `ymd()` first. `"2026-04-10" - "2026-03-15"` is an error.
- **Relying on alphabetical order.** "High, Low, Medium" is rarely what you want. Set the order with `fct_relevel()` or `fct_infreq()`.

## Summary

- stringr functions start with `str_`. Use `str_squish()`, `str_to_title()`, `str_replace()` and `str_detect()` to clean and search text.
- lubridate parses dates with `ymd()`, `dmy()` and `mdy()`. Pull out parts with `year()`, `month()` and `wday()`, and round with `floor_date()`.
- Subtracting dates gives the days between them. Add time with `days()` and `months()`.
- forcats controls factor levels: `fct_relevel()` sets the order, `fct_infreq()` sorts by frequency, `fct_recode()` renames and `fct_lump_n()` groups rare levels.
